extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, political writers, and the educated public (18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and analysis for diagnosing causes of public disorder and for constructing political argument/strategy—both as guidance for statesmen and as a model for persuasive political pamphleteering. Emphasizes diagnosis, timing, rhetoric, and tactics of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the temper of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: “The temper of the people amongst whom he presides ought therefore to be the first study of a statesman.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statesman must first learn the prevailing disposition and moods of the populace; knowledge of that temper enables judicious management. This knowledge is attainable unless one has an interest in remaining ignorant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ordinary complaints from true political grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: “True political sagacity manifests itself in distinguishing that complaint which only characterizes the general infirmity of human nature, from those which are symptoms of the particular distemperature of our own air and season.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the perennial tendency of people to grumble with specific systemic problems; diagnose whether a complaint is timeless human infirmity or an indicator of a current constitutional or governmental fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume in favor of the people in disputes with rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: When disputes arise between the people and their rulers, the presumption is at least upon a par in favor of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given that the people have little to gain from disorder, widespread discontent should be taken seriously as likely signaling real grievance; it is often easier to change an administration than to reform a whole people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of discontent indicates systemic problems
rubrics_metrics.description: “When popular discontents have been very prevalent, it may well be affirmed and supported, that there has been generally something found amiss in the constitution, or in the conduct of government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High levels of popular unrest are a diagnostic signal pointing to faults in institutions or governance rather than merely to private malice or isolated agitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using particular punishments as cures for systemic mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: “Particular punishments are the cure for accidental distempers in the state; they inflame rather than allay those heats which arise from the settled mismanagement of the government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor remedies to the cause: punitive measures aimed at individuals help with isolated disorders but exacerbate deep, structural grievances. Use firmness only when accompanied by wise, proportionate policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firmness must be accompanied by wisdom; avoid inconstancy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Firmness is then only a virtue when it accompanies the most perfect wisdom. In truth, inconstancy is a sort of natural corrective of folly and ignorance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong measures are effective only when guided by sound judgment; arbitrary shifts or mere show of firmness without understanding will worsen problems or be self-correcting in the public mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct temporal inference when attributing policy effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy effects must be judged only after the earliest time at which they could operate (e.g. look for effects in 'the year of first possible operation'), and not from the year the regulation was made if it could not yet take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing economic or political outcomes to measures before they could plausibly have acted. Use appropriate lagging, inspect multi-year series (not single-year snapshots), and choose consistent baseline years to prevent misleading causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple causes and avoid simplistic attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: “Other causes had their operation, without doubt. In what degree each cause produced its effect, it is hard to determine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When outcomes change, assess the range of plausible causes and estimate their relative contributions rather than claiming a single decisive cause from limited data or partisan inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize subtle forms of influence over overt prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: “The power of the crown ... has grown up anew, with much more strength, and far less odium, under the name of Influence. An influence, which operated without noise and without violence... was an admirable substitute for a prerogative.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and evaluate quiet, systemic mechanisms of power (patronage, influence, institutional manipulation) rather than only obvious legal prerogatives; these can be more effective and less publicly resented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to schemes that separate visible administration from real advisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan element: to 'separate the court from the ministry' so the latter is ostensible and responsible while real advisers remain removed from danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize structural tactics for concentrating power: creating a visible, scapegoated administration while decision-making power resides elsewhere undermines accountability and shifts responsibility away from the real sources of policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect organization of a pro-court party detached from administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan element: form 'a party under these leaders ... in favor of the court against the ministry' that holds emoluments and is independent of ostensible administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for the deliberate creation of client parties whose loyalty is to personal favor rather than public interest; such parties change incentive structures and weaken representative ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize methods to habituate Parliament to acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan element: 'to bring Parliament to an acquiescence ... by means of a discipline ... that body was to be habituated to the most opposite interests, and the most discordant politics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tactics aimed at disciplining or blunting parliamentary independence (e.g., loading membership with dependents, eroding prestige). Effective political critique should identify how procedural and cultural changes produce legislative acquiescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda and pamphleteering to shape public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: “To recommend this system to the people, a perspective view of the court, gorgeously painted, and finely illuminated from within, was exhibited to the gaping multitude ... in a pamphlet which had all the appearance of a manifesto.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical instruments—pamphlets, satire, manifestos—can be crafted to present a polished image that masks underlying aims. Evaluate the rhetorical form, audience appeal, and possible hypocrisy of such pieces when judging political communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undermine rival leaders and connections to consolidate personal influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactic observed: 'they proceeded ... to destroy everything of strength which did not derive its principal nourishment from the immediate pleasure of the court'—removing leaders and proscribing their adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to deliberate purges or proscription of established leaders and networks as a method of consolidating centralized influence; such moves may destabilize government and are diagnostic of a deliberate reconfiguration of power.
